title: The house-builder
hookLine: craving named and seen; the rafters broken, the ridgepole shattered (Dhammapada 153–154)

cards: The same argument, for the tenth time. The same late-night snack. The same reason for not calling someone back.
Then one day, instead of just doing it again, you catch it in the act. Oh. There it is.
That's the thing that keeps building this. Tradition says that when the Buddha woke, the first words he spoke were a short poem. Not a sermon.
Not a rule. A poem to someone he'd been looking for, for a very long time, and finally, he'd found him.

teach.h: A HOUSE BUILT AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: The poem is in the Dhammapada, verses one fifty-three and one fifty-four, and it pictures life after life as a house built again and again.
Through many births, the Buddha says, he ran on, looking for the builder of this house, and birth again and again was painful.
Then, in Max Müller's translation from 1881, he speaks directly to the builder: "maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again."
Tabernacle is Müller's old word for the house: a dwelling, a tent. And then: "All thy rafters are broken, thy ridge-pole is sundered."
So who is the house-builder? The Buddhist commentaries answer: craving. Tanha, the thirst from day nine, the wanting that keeps building a self and a life around it, over and over.
The rafters, they say, are the other stains of the mind. The ridgepole, the beam at the very top that holds up the whole roof, is ignorance. And look at the first verb.
Before anything is broken, the builder is seen; the rafters fall after. That's this whole week in one poem: a seat of grass, a vow to stay, Mara's army, the earth as witness, three watches, and dawn.
And at the end, one quiet sentence to the one who'd been building the whole time.

how: Dhammapada 153–154 are memorized and chanted in Theravada communities, whose tradition holds they were the Buddha's first words after awakening, and teachers use the house-builder to explain craving as the source of rebirth.

o: craving, which builds life after life
a monk who built the first monastery
the god who built the world and us

games.q: what's inside the poem — tap the pairs.
p: the other stains of the mind

s: the house-builder in the poem is a god who made the world
the commentaries say the builder is craving, which builds life after life.
Theravada tradition holds these verses were the Buddha's first words after awakening
Dhammapada 153–154, a poem to the house-builder.
in the poem, the rafters break before the builder is seen
the builder is seen first; then the rafters are broken and the ridge-pole sundered.

games.q: after many births, you finally find the one who keeps building your house. what do you say?
o: thou hast been seen; thou shalt not build again.
I'll fight you to the end.
games.why: he names the builder, craving, and tells it: you've been seen. the rafters are broken, the ridgepole shattered.

practice: Think of one habit you've already started to see through, something you used to do without noticing: hitting snooze, interrupting, checking the fridge when bored.

Picture it as a small builder busy with hammer and nails, and silently speak to it the way the poem does, not angrily, just clearly: I see you. Notice whether seeing it changes anything, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The house-builder. Craving, which builds life after life, seen at last by the Buddha: its rafters broken, its ridgepole shattered.

orig.note: Pali: house-builder (gaha, house + kāraka, maker), the name for craving in Dhammapada 153–154.

carryVoice: Your line: house-builder, you are seen. Day fifty-six closes the night under the tree.
